title: Serve JSON over HTTP
summary: Replace a plain-text handler with a routed JSON response and reason about headers.

scenario.briefing: The order endpoint returns a plain string with no content type. Return a JSON object for /orders/ and keep the route table explicit.

hints: Set the Content-Type header before writing the body.

misconceptions.description: Writing a plain string without a content type.
misconceptions.testDescription: The handler writes a JSON response.
misconceptions.feedback: Set Content-Type to application/json and encode a value. A bare string does not describe the response shape.
Headers after WriteHeader are ignored, not fatal. Set them before the first write.

misconceptions.description: Believing net/http runs handlers one at a time.
misconceptions.feedback: Each request runs in its own goroutine. Shared maps need a mutex or another synchronization mechanism.

sections.title: Handlers write a response
sections.body: An http.HandlerFunc receives a ResponseWriter and a Request. Write headers before the first body byte. Once WriteHeader is called, later header changes are ignored. Set Content-Type before encoding the body.

sections.title: A mux routes by pattern
sections.body: http.ServeMux matches the longest registered pattern. A pattern ending in a slash matches a subtree, while an exact pattern matches one path. Register handlers on the mux and pass it to http.ListenAndServe.

sections.title: Servers need timeouts and error handling
sections.body: The default server has no read or write timeout, which lets slow clients hold connections. Configure timeouts on http.Server and handle encoding errors. Handlers run concurrently, so shared state needs synchronization.

steps.prompt: A handler calls WriteHeader(200), writes the body, and then sets another header. What happens to the later header?

quiz.explanation: The status and headers are flushed when the first body write happens. Later header changes do not reach the client.
